title: Gargi's second arrow
hook: the woman who was silenced stands up again, like a warrior stringing a bow, with two questions

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka asked about the thread and the inner ruler, the one whose body the earth is. Your line was the inner ruler lives in every being.
screen: `THE INNER RULER LIVES IN EVERY BEING.`

segments.voice: Gargi stands up again. Two days ago she was told: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off, and she sat down. This time she speaks to the whole room first. Honored scholars, I'll ask him two questions. If he answers them, none of you will ever beat him. Then she turns to Yajnavalkya. As a warrior's son from Kashi or Videha strings his unstrung bow, takes two sharp arrows in his hand and rises to fight, so I rise against you with two questions. Answer them.
screen: `SHE STANDS UP AGAIN.` → `A WARRIOR STRINGING HIS BOW.` → `TWO QUESTIONS, LIKE TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First arrow. What is above the sky and below the earth and between the two, what people call past, present and future: on what is that woven? On space, Gargi. She bows. Honor to you, Yajnavalkya, for that answer. Get ready for the second. Second arrow. And on what is space woven? This time he doesn't stop her. He answers. That, Gargi, is what the knowers of Brahman call the imperishable, the akshara. It is neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long. Without shadow, without taste or smell, without eye or ear, without inside or outside. It eats nothing, and nothing eats it. And yet at its command the sun and moon are held apart, earth and sky are held apart, and rivers run from the snowy mountains. Here's the teaching, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest. Brahman, the one reality, isn't one more thing in the world, not even the biggest thing. It's what everything is woven on, so the Upanishad describes it almost entirely by what it isn't. That's how many Hindus can bow to a murti of Krishna or Durga at home and still say God has no edges. As many teachers put it, the form is where you meet God, not a fence around God. And Gargi turns to the room. Count yourselves lucky if you get away by bowing to him. None of you will beat him. Then she falls silent, on her own terms. Tradition remembers her as a brahmavadini, a woman who spoke of Brahman, and she drew out the hardest answer of the day.
screen: `FIRST ARROW: WOVEN ON SPACE.` · `SECOND ARROW: ON WHAT IS SPACE WOVEN?` · `THE IMPERISHABLE: ONLY WHAT IT ISN'T.` · `THE FORM IS WHERE YOU MEET GOD.` · then, large: `BRAHMAN ISN'T ONE MORE THING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let each thing you notice be named and set down: a sound, not that; a sensation in the knee, not that; a thought, not that. Not coarse, like the chair; not fine, like the thought. Keep setting things down, gently, without looking for what's left, and rest in the room the setting-down makes.
Akshara. The imperishable, what doesn't wear away. The same word means a syllable or a letter, and in Gargi's question, it's what even space is woven on.
Your line: brahman isn't one more thing. Next, someone asks how many gods there are. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: The akshara passage is studied in Vedanta as one of the Upanishads' great descriptions of Brahman by negation; Gargi's two questions are often retold in Hindu teaching as the moment the debate turns.

original.note: Sanskrit akṣara: a (not) + kṣara (perishing): the imperishable; also a syllable or letter.

Gargi.meaning: the woman scholar who rises with two questions, like arrows

Yajnavalkya.meaning: the sage who answers the challengers in Janaka's court

Kashi.meaning: an ancient kingdom, named in Gargi's warrior image

akshara.meaning: the imperishable; the same word means a syllable or letter

Brahman.meaning: the great reality the Upanishads seek to know

murti.meaning: a sacred image of God, honored in homes and temples

brahmavadini.meaning: a woman who speaks of Brahman; what tradition calls Gargi
